proof:
# Radial layer barriers for arbitrary compatible fibers

This is a strictification theorem for a specified affine interior section.
It does not assert that such a section exists for every mixed source, and
it does not assert a new halfspace-depth lower bound.

Let P be a finite nonempty subset of Z^n with

    conv(P) intersect Z^n = P.

For each z in P let K_z be a full-dimensional compact convex body in
R^d, d>=1. Assume the family is compatible: for every representation
z=sum_p alpha_p p, alpha_p>=0, sum alpha_p=1,

    sum_p alpha_p K_p subset K_z.                         (1)

Suppose that there is an AFFINE map q:aff(P)->R^d satisfying
q(z) in int K_z for every z. There are arbitrarily close compatible
families L_z with all of the following properties:

* Their total d-volume is exactly the original total volume.
* Every L_z is a positive homothet of K_z about q(z).
* Every interpolation at a base z by OTHER bases is uniformly strictly
  inside L_z. Consequently there is an open neighborhood of independent
  Hausdorff perturbations retaining exactly the prescribed integer fibers.
* For every fixed u!=0, the individual fraction in
  H_u={ (z,x): u.(x-q(z))>=0 } is unchanged in each fiber.
  If that fraction is independent of z, the total mass of H_u is exactly
  unchanged as well. This holds simultaneously for any collection of
  such directions having the specified equal-fraction property.

The directions need not be coordinate directions; q makes these ambient
halfspaces oblique in the original coordinates. The lattice bases remain
unchanged throughout.

## 1. A finite radial barrier

The affine shear x->x-q(z) has fiber Jacobian one and preserves all
convex interpolation relations. Work in these coordinates, so 0 is
interior to every K_z. Fix numbers 0<m<=M such that, for all unit u,

    m <= h_z(u) <= M,   h_z(u)=max_(x in K_z) u.x.         (2)

Finiteness and interior membership provide such numbers.

Remove the vertices of conv(P), then the vertices of the convex hull of
the remaining set, and continue until nothing remains. The layer index
ell(z) is zero for the first removed vertices, one for the next ones,
and so on; let L=max ell(z). All convex hulls and their vertices are
taken in their own affine spans. The process terminates because each
nonempty finite set has a vertex.

For every nonvertex z of conv(P), let A_z be the compact polytope of its
convex representations by P without z. It is nonempty. Take all its
finitely many extreme points, for all such z, and let alpha_* be the
smallest positive coordinate occurring among them. Then alpha_*>0.
If there are no nonvertices, skip the barrier construction: compatibility
already has no nontrivial excluded-target constraints.

Set

    delta=min(1/2,alpha_* m/M),
    b_z=1-delta^ell(z),
    kappa=(1-delta)delta^L >0.                            (3)

Claim: for every extreme representation alpha in A_z and every unit u,

    b_z h_z(u)-sum_p alpha_p b_p h_p(u)
       >= b_z [h_z(u)-sum_p alpha_p h_p(u)] + m kappa.    (4)

To prove it, write H=sum alpha_p h_p(u), so m<=H<=M, and introduce
the probability weights p_p=alpha_p h_p(u)/H. The base z lies in some
layer ell>=1. In its representation at least one positive coefficient
belongs to an earlier layer. Otherwise it would be a convex combination
of other points in the set in which it was a vertex, a contradiction.
That earlier-layer weight p_p is at least alpha_* m/M>=delta. Since
b is increasing in the layer index,

    sum_p p_p b_p
       <= delta(1-delta^(ell-1))+(1-delta)(1-delta^L)
        = b_z-kappa.                                    (5)

Multiplication by H proves (4). Compatibility gives
h_z(u)-H>=0. This argument is uniform over all directions, and uses
only finite extreme representations, not a choice of a favorable
direction for a given relation.

## 2. Strict compatible radial expansions

For epsilon>0 let

    J_z(epsilon)=(1+epsilon b_z)K_z.

Using (4), for every extreme excluded-target representation,

    h_(J_z)(u)-sum_p alpha_p h_(J_p)(u)
      >= (1+epsilon b_z)[h_z(u)-sum_p alpha_p h_p(u)]
            +epsilon m kappa
      >= epsilon m kappa.                               (6)

For an arbitrary alpha in A_z the same inequality follows by expressing
alpha as a convex combination of extreme points; the left side is
affine in alpha. Thus every excluded-target interpolant plus the ball
of radius epsilon m kappa is contained in J_z.

A representation having positive self-weight can be reduced to one
without that weight: if alpha_z<1, divide the other weights by
1-alpha_z. They still represent z. Compatibility for this reduced
representation implies compatibility for the original one. The case
alpha_z=1 is tautological. Hence the entire expanded family is compatible.

Let w_z=vol_d(K_z)>0, W=sum w_z, and define

    lambda(epsilon)= [W/sum_z (1+epsilon b_z)^d w_z]^(1/d),
    L_z(epsilon)=lambda(epsilon) J_z(epsilon).            (7)

The common dilation preserves every compatibility relation. The total
volume is exactly W, and every excluded-target support gap is at least

    g=lambda(epsilon) epsilon m kappa>0.                  (8)

As epsilon tends to zero, lambda tends to one and every L_z tends to
K_z in Hausdorff distance. Map back through the original affine shear;
these are precisely homotheties about q(z).

## 3. An actual neighborhood of independent fiber perturbations

Fix epsilon>0. In the centered coordinates every L_z contains the ball
of radius lambda m. Choose

    0<eta<min(g/4,lambda m/2).

If d_H(T_z,L_z)<eta for independently chosen compact convex bodies T_z,
then their support functions differ by less than eta on the unit sphere.
Each T_z still contains a positive ball. For every excluded-target
representation,

    h_(T_z)(u)-sum_p alpha_p h_(T_p)(u)>g-2eta>0.           (9)

This proves a uniform strict containment of all corresponding
Minkowski interpolants. The self-weight reduction proves compatibility
for every representation, so

    C(T)=conv union_(z in P) ({z} times T_z)

has EXACTLY the fibers T_z at P. Its projection is conv(P), so lattice
completeness excludes all other integer bases. The hull is compact and
has nonempty interior in aff(P) times R^d. If aff(P)=R^n it is an ambient
convex body. The lower-rank case is only a relative-body assertion here;
no unproved ambient completion is needed.

If all bases were original vertices, there are no excluded-target
representations. Taking L_z=K_z already gives the same independent
neighborhood assertion, using any sufficiently small eta preserving
positive interior balls. There is no need to define alpha_* in that case.

## 4. Exactly preserved cap budgets

The centered cap {u.x>=0} is invariant under every positive radial
dilation. Its hyperplane boundary has zero d-volume. Therefore with
s_z=lambda(1+epsilon b_z),

    vol_d(L_z intersect {u.x>=0})
        =s_z^d vol_d(K_z intersect {u.x>=0}).               (10)

In particular each individual fraction is unchanged. If those fractions
all equal p_u, then (7) and (10) give the exact mixed identity

    sum_z vol_d(L_z intersect H_u)=p_u W
                                 =sum_z vol_d(K_z intersect H_u). (11)

Each additional direction with constant original fraction satisfies its
own identity at the same time. No finiteness assumption on that set of
directions is needed. Formula (11) does not assert invariance for a
direction whose fractions differ between fibers, or for a cap whose
boundary does not contain the entire affine section q.

## 5. Scope and relation to the homothetic construction

The construction permits unrelated convex shapes: compatibility and a
common affine interior section are its only geometric hypotheses.
For example, any compatible centrally symmetric family about an affine
center field has fraction1/2 in every H_u, and the flat stage preserves
all of these cap budgets simultaneously even when its fibers are not
homothetic. This does not produce an improving volume/cap variation in
that example: two opposite budgets already bound total mass.

For homothetic centered simplices it recovers a flat strictification of
the shared canonical budgets, by a different finite-layer mechanism than
quadratic perturbation of their radii. The subsequent positive physical
second variation from the existing shared-canonical theorem then still
applies. For arbitrary shapes, no such second variation is claimed.

No arbitrary convex source is asserted to admit the affine interior
section required here. In particular, arbitrary locations of fibers at
exposed integer vertices can obstruct that hypothesis. The theorem
also does not handle intrinsic direction changes or zero-volume fibers;
those are outside its explicitly full-d fiber scope.
